title: ARIES Recovery
description: Master the ARIES recovery algorithm: analysis, redo, and undo phases, LSN tracking, compensation log records, fuzzy checkpoints, and physiological logging.

segments.text: A database crashes mid-transaction. Some committed transactions might not have been flushed to disk. Some uncommitted transactions might have partially written to disk. ARIES — Algorithms for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics — is the gold standard recovery algorithm used by DB2, SQL Server, and PostgreSQL. It guarantees correctness after any crash.

Write-Ahead Logging is the foundation. Before any data page modification hits disk, the corresponding log record must be written to the WAL first. Each log record has a Log Sequence Number — a monotonically increasing identifier. The WAL is the source of truth — even if data pages are corrupted, the WAL can reconstruct the correct state.

Analysis phase: scan the WAL from the last checkpoint forward. Build a dirty page table — which pages were modified but not flushed. Build an active transaction table — which transactions were in progress at crash time. This tells recovery which pages need redo and which transactions need undo. No data pages are read during analysis.

Redo phase: replay ALL logged changes from the oldest dirty page's LSN forward, including uncommitted transactions. For each log record, check if the page's on-disk LSN is less than the log record's LSN. If yes, redo the change. This brings the database to the exact state at crash time — both committed and uncommitted changes.

Undo phase: roll back all uncommitted transactions by processing their log records in reverse order. For each undo, write a Compensation Log Record — a log record that records the undo operation itself. CLRs are redo-only — if the system crashes during recovery, it won't undo the undo. This is what makes ARIES crash-safe during recovery.
The system crashes during the undo phase of recovery. When it restarts, it starts recovery again. How does ARIES prevent undoing the same changes twice? What role do Compensation Log Records play?
segments.thought_prompt: How does ARIES handle a crash during recovery? Why are CLRs essential for correctness?

segments.text: Fuzzy checkpoints avoid stopping the database. Instead of forcing all dirty pages to disk, a fuzzy checkpoint writes the dirty page table and active transaction table to the WAL. Dirty pages are flushed asynchronously in the background. Recovery starts from the checkpoint's LSN — older log records can be garbage collected.

Physiological logging records changes at the page level but with logical descriptions. Instead of logging 'set byte 4096 on page 42 to 0xFF', log 'insert key 7 into B-tree page 42'. This makes logs smaller and allows page-level concurrency without full page locking. It's the middle ground between physical and logical logging.

Recovery time depends on WAL length since the last checkpoint. Checkpoint every five minutes means at most five minutes of WAL to replay. But frequent checkpoints increase I/O during normal operation. PostgreSQL's default checkpoint interval is five minutes or after one gigabyte of WAL. Tune based on your acceptable recovery time versus steady-state performance tradeoff.

Your database has a five-minute checkpoint interval and processes one million transactions per minute. After a crash, recovery takes forty-five minutes — too long. How would you reduce recovery time without impacting normal throughput?
segments.thought_prompt: Reduce 45-minute recovery time for a high-throughput database. What tuning options exist?

segments.text: ARIES recovery guarantees correctness through three phases: analysis builds the recovery state, redo replays all changes to crash-time state, and undo rolls back uncommitted transactions with CLRs for crash-safety during recovery. Fuzzy checkpoints bound recovery time, and physiological logging balances log size with concurrency. This is the algorithm that makes ACID possible.
